`const message = `${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}`` is always a non-empty string, so `message || t("unable_to_add_guests")` never falls back. Users see strings like "FORBIDDEN: you_do_not_have_permission" (and `undefined: ...` when `err.data` is missing) rather than a localized message.

MultiEmail imports from the @calcom/ui barrel that re-exports it, creating a cycle

`packages/ui/index.tsx` now exports `MultiEmail` from `./form/MultiEmailLazy`, while `MultiEmail.tsx` imports `Button, EmailField, Icon, Tooltip` from `@calcom/ui` — the same barrel. This circular dependency can cause undefined components at module-init time in some bundling/SSR orders. Import directly from the component paths like other files in `packages/ui/form` do.

No tests for the new addGuests handler

The handler contains non-trivial authorization, dedup/blacklist filtering and calendar/email side effects, but no unit tests were added. At minimum the permission branches (organizer / attendee / team role) and the duplicate-and-blacklist filtering should be covered to prevent regressions in an endpoint that writes attendees and sends mail.

Organizer subject dereferences attendees[0] and uses an empty guest name

`this.calEvent.attendees[0].name` will throw if the attendee list is empty, and newly added guests are created with `name: ""`, so the subject can render as "Guests Added:  with  at ..." when the first attendee is a name-less guest. Guard the access and fall back to the attendee email.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
deleteMany OR branch deletes reminders of all methods, not just SMS

The new OR branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` constraint, so this SMS-only cron will delete EMAIL and WHATSAPP WorkflowReminder rows whenever their retryCount exceeds 1. Since retryCount is a shared column that other schedulers may also increment in the future (and the field is generic), this can silently destroy pending email/WhatsApp reminders. Add the method filter inside the OR branch.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).

false_positives.candidate:
Failure paths that never increment retryCount keep retrying forever

retryCount is only incremented when `twilio.scheduleSMS` returns falsy or throws. If `message` is empty/null or `sendTo` is missing (e.g. attendee without a phone number), the `if (message?.length ... && sendTo)` block is skipped entirely, the reminder stays `scheduled: false`, and the cron will keep picking it up every run until the scheduledDate passes — exactly the behaviour this PR intends to stop. Increment retryCount (or mark it) in that else case too.

deleteMany on retryCount has no supporting index

The new delete condition filters on `retryCount > 1` with no method/scheduledDate constraint and there is no index covering retryCount, so each cron run forces a full scan of WorkflowReminder (a high-volume table). Consider restricting the predicate to SMS + existing indexed columns or adding an appropriate index.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead branches in getBaseConditions

`getAuthorizationConditions()` always resolves to a `Prisma.Sql` (never null/undefined), so the `else if (filterConditions)` and final `return NOTHING_CONDITION` branches are unreachable. This hides the intent and could mask a future regression where auth conditions legitimately become empty — an empty auth condition would then fall through to returning only filter conditions, which would be an authorization bypass. Simplify to `authConditions` + optional filter, and assert auth is always present.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

false_positives.candidate:
Caching tests deleted without replacement

The `describe("Caching")` block covering `cachedAuthConditions` / `cachedFilterConditions` memoization was removed entirely, but the caching logic in `getAuthorizationConditions`/`getFilterConditions` still exists (including the subtle `=== undefined` check needed because filter conditions may legitimately be `null`). Regressions that cause the conditions to be rebuilt on every call, or that break the null-caching case, are now untested.

Constructor option type widened, losing discriminated-union safety

The constructor parameter type changed from the zod-derived discriminated union `InsightsBookingServiceOptions` to the loose `InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions` where `teamId` is optional for every scope. Callers can now pass `{ scope: "team", userId, orgId }` without a `teamId` and it compiles; at runtime the zod validation fails silently and `options` becomes `null`, so the service returns `1=0` and the caller sees zero rows instead of a type error or explicit failure. Keep the union type (or at least surface the validation error).

Public `findMany` removed without updating callers

`findMany(findManyArgs)` was the only query-executing method of `InsightsBookingService` and has been replaced by `getBaseConditions()` returning a `Prisma.Sql` fragment. No other files in this PR are updated, so any existing consumer calling `insightsBookingService.findMany(...)` will fail to compile / break at runtime. Either keep a `findMany` wrapper that executes `$queryRaw` against "BookingTimeStatusDenormalized", or update all call sites in the same PR.

Tests assert exact SQL string equality, making them brittle and weak

Comparing the returned `Prisma.Sql` with `toEqual(Prisma.sql`...`)` asserts both the exact text fragments and parameter values. Any harmless reformatting/parenthesization change in the service breaks the suite, while semantic correctness (does the SQL actually restrict rows correctly?) is still untested for the team/org scopes. Consider asserting behaviour via `$queryRaw` for at least the team and org authorization scopes, as is done in the `getBaseConditions` test.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateManyByCredentialId called with empty data relies on implicit @updatedAt and adds a write per cache refresh

`SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` is intended to bump `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt`, but it passes an empty data object, so it only has an effect if the model declares `@updatedAt`; otherwise it is a silent no-op while still issuing an UPDATE over every selected calendar of the credential on each cache population. The PR notes also state this value is never consumed by the frontend. Either set the field explicitly (`updatedAt: new Date()`) and document the consumer, or drop the call.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sed -i '' is macOS-only and ENV_FILE path is cwd-dependent

`sed -i '' -E ...` fails on GNU sed (Linux), where `-i ''` is interpreted as an empty script file name, so the script cannot update .env on Linux/CI. Additionally `ENV_FILE="../.env"` is relative to the current working directory, so running the script from the repo root writes/creates a `.env` outside the repository.

true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
deleteCache throws plain Error instead of TRPCError

Throwing `new Error("Credential not found or access denied")` from a tRPC handler surfaces as an INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR (HTTP 500) rather than a 403/404, and the message may be scrubbed in production. Use `TRPCError({ code: "NOT_FOUND" | "FORBIDDEN" })` so the client can distinguish an authorization failure from a server fault.

true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Timestamp hardcoded to en-US locale

`new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", …)` formats the cache timestamp with US month/day ordering and 12-hour clock regardless of the user's locale/time format preference, producing confusing dates for non-US users. Use the user's locale (e.g. from `useLocale()`) or the existing date formatting helpers.

false_positives.candidate:
Cache status ignores expiresAt, so expired caches are reported as fresh

`getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` groups all CalendarCache rows for the credential with no `expiresAt` filter. The UI then shows "Cache Status / Last updated: …" for credentials whose cache entries are already expired and will no longer be served, which misleads users into believing caching is active. Filter on `expiresAt: { gte: new Date() }` (or surface expiry explicitly).

Credential ownership check misses team/delegation credentials

The handler only matches `credential.userId === user.id`. Credentials attached to a team (userId null, teamId set) or delegation-derived credentials will never match, so deleting their cache always fails; conversely there is no check that the user is allowed to act on team credentials at all. Consider mirroring the authorization logic used by `viewer.credentials.delete` (user OR team admin/owner) so behaviour is consistent and complete.

Migration header comment contradicts the statement

The generated warning says the column was added "without a default value. This is not possible if the table is not empty", yet the statement adds `DEFAULT NOW()`. Leaving the stale warning in place is confusing for anyone auditing migrations; remove or correct it.

No tests for new cache-status enrichment or deleteCache handler

The new `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` repository method, the enrichment in connectedCalendarsHandler, and the deleteCache handler (including its authorization branch) have no unit tests. Given the authorization check in deleteCache guards data deletion, at least a test covering a credential owned by another user should be added.

deleteCache success does not invalidate the connectedCalendars query

The disconnect mutation invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`, but the deleteCache mutation only calls the optional `onSuccess` prop. In the Alert branch of SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper (and anywhere `onChanged` is not passed) nothing invalidates the query, so the dropdown keeps showing a stale "Last updated" timestamp for a cache that was just deleted. Invalidate `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` in the mutation's onSettled.

dev:cron switched to npx tsx without adding tsx as a dependency

`npx tsx cron-tester.ts` relies on npx fetching `tsx` from the network at run time (and may prompt for install), while `ts-node` remains a devDependency. Add `tsx` to devDependencies and invoke it via the local binary for reproducible, offline-capable runs.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
try/catch cannot catch failures from async reminder deletions

`originalRescheduledBooking.workflowReminders.forEach(...)` invokes `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`/`deleteScheduledSMSReminder` without awaiting; the returned promises escape the surrounding try/catch. Although both helpers swallow their own errors internally today, any throw outside their try (or a future change) becomes an unhandled rejection rather than the logged error the code intends. The same pattern exists in `handleCancelBooking.ts` and `bookings.tsx`; consider `await Promise.all(...)`.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
immediateDelete path cancels at SendGrid but never removes the WorkflowReminder row

When `immediateDelete` is true the function POSTs the cancel to SendGrid and returns early without deleting (or flagging) the `workflowReminder` row. Callers that previously deleted the row themselves no longer do (e.g. `handleNewBooking.ts` for the original rescheduled booking). The result is rows left behind with `scheduled: true` and a referenceId that has already been cancelled; they linger until the cron's `deleteMany(scheduledDate <= now)` cleanup, and the cron's `cancelled` sweep will never touch them. At minimum this is stale data for reporting/queries; it also makes the semantics of the function inconsistent with the `!referenceId` branch, which does delete the row.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
Cancellation sweep does not filter by method and aborts all remaining cancellations on first error

`remindersToCancel` queries only `cancelled: true` without `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL`, so any non-email reminder that ever gets flagged cancelled will have its Twilio SID posted to the SendGrid `scheduled_sends` endpoint. More importantly the whole `for` loop is inside a single try/catch: if one SendGrid request fails (invalid/expired batch id, rate limit), the loop exits and every remaining reminder in this run is left uncancelled, so their emails may be sent before the next cron tick (the window is only 1 hour while the cron runs every 15 min, so a couple of failed runs is enough to leak reminders). Each reminder should be cancelled/deleted in its own try/catch and the query should be scoped to EMAIL.

Malformed import (missing trailing comma) and type-only imports converted to value imports

The import block now reads `  TimeUnit,\n  Prisma\n} from "@prisma/client";` with no trailing comma and inconsistent formatting, which will fail the repo's prettier/lint check. Additionally `Prisma` and `PrismaPromise` were switched from `import type` to value imports here (and `App`/`Credential`/`EventTypeCustomInput`/`Prisma` in `handleNewBooking.ts`), which pulls type-only symbols into the runtime import graph unnecessarily.

SMS reminder row is not deleted if twilio.cancelSMS throws

`twilio.cancelSMS(referenceId)` and `prisma.workflowReminder.delete` share one try block. If cancelling fails (e.g. the message already left the queue, or a transient Twilio error), the DB row is never deleted and the reminder stays in the table indefinitely with `scheduled: true`. Deleting the row should be done regardless of the cancel result.

SendGrid client API key is never set in this handler

`sgMail.setApiKey(sendgridAPIKey)` is called at module load, but `client` (`@sendgrid/client`) has no `client.setApiKey(...)` call in this file, unlike `emailReminderManager.ts` which does both. The new cancellation requests (and the existing `/v3/mail/batch` call) therefore go out unauthenticated and will fail with 401, meaning cancelled reminders are never actually cancelled — the exact bug this PR is meant to fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Eagerly created import promises can produce unhandled rejections

Because each `import(...)` promise is created at module load, any app module that throws during initialization (e.g. missing env/app keys) produces a rejected promise that nobody is awaiting at that moment. In Node this surfaces as an unhandled promise rejection and can crash the process (or at minimum log a fatal warning), even for apps the request never touches. With lazy thunks the rejection would only occur where it is awaited and handled.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
async callback inside forEach escapes the try/catch and is never awaited

Changing the `forEach` callback to `async` means the returned promises are discarded: the enclosing `try/catch` can no longer catch failures of `getCalendar`/`deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` (they become unhandled rejections), and the function returns/sends the reschedule email before the calendar/video events are actually deleted. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (ref) => ...))` instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Dynamic imports are invoked eagerly, defeating the lazy-loading goal

The appStore object calls `import("./applecalendar")` etc. at module-evaluation time, so every app package is loaded as soon as `@calcom/app-store` is imported. The only difference from the previous static imports is that consumers now have to `await` the values; nothing is actually deferred (bundle size and startup cost are unchanged, and in webpack all chunks are requested immediately). To get real async loading the values must be thunks, e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`, with call sites doing `await appStore[key]()`.

Noisy info log of CalendarService on every getCalendar call

`log.info("calendarApp", calendarApp.lib.CalendarService)` logs the service class on every calendar resolution, which now happens on every booking/cancel/availability path. This is debug-level noise in production logs and should be removed or downgraded.

Unused awaited calendar in recurring branch

`const calendar = await getCalendar(calendarCredential)` is computed before the branch, but in the recurring path a new `calendar` is fetched inside the loop, so the outer one is unused. This performs an unnecessary credential/calendar instantiation (and now an extra module load) on every recurring cancellation.

async callback inside forEach escapes the try/catch and is never awaited

Same issue as the vital reschedule: making the `forEach` callback `async` means its promise is dropped, so errors from `getCalendar`/`deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` bypass the surrounding `try/catch` and become unhandled rejections, and the function continues (sending emails, returning true) before the external events are deleted. Use `Promise.all` over `map` and await it.

getCalendarCredentials now returns a Promise in the `calendar` field, breaking external consumers

`getCalendar` became async, but `getCalendarCredentials` still stores its result synchronously, so `item.calendar` is now a `Promise<Calendar | null>` instead of `Calendar | null`. `getConnectedCalendars` was updated to await it, but any other caller of `getCalendarCredentials` that uses `.calendar` directly (e.g. to call `listCalendars()`/`getAvailability()`) will now be operating on a Promise and fail at runtime. Either make `getCalendarCredentials` async and resolve the calendars, or audit/update all consumers.

requestReschedule fires calendar/video deletions without awaiting them

The `forEach` callback is now `async` and awaits `getCalendar`, but the loop does not await the resulting promises. The mutation proceeds to send the reschedule email and webhooks and returns while deletions are still pending; in a serverless environment the function may terminate before they run, leaving stale calendar/video events, and any error becomes an unhandled rejection. Collect the promises with `map` and `await Promise.all`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours end boundary computed from slot start, ignoring event length

`const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` duplicates the `start` computation instead of using `slotEndTime`. The check `end > workingHour.endTime` therefore never accounts for the event duration, so a slot that starts inside working hours but ends after them is treated as available.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dayjs objects compared with === (always false)

`if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset,'minutes') === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset,'minutes'))` compares two freshly created Dayjs object references, which is never true. The intent (detecting a zero-length override, i.e. a day marked unavailable) is never reached, so days blocked out via a start==end override are still offered as bookable.

false_positives.candidate:
Any date override on the slot's day short-circuits the busy-time check

In `checkIfIsAvailable`, after the date-override loop, `if (dateOverrideExist) return true;` returns availability immediately whenever a date override exists for the slot's day. This skips the `busy.every(...)` check below, so existing bookings, calendar busy times and buffers are completely ignored on days that have a date override, allowing double bookings on those days.

Date-override day comparison uses local-time formatting and a hand-rolled offset

`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset,'minutes').format('YYYY MM DD')` parses the stored UTC override date in the server's local timezone and then shifts it by `dayjs.tz(date.start, organizerTimeZone).utcOffset() * -1`, which reinterprets the UTC instant as organizer wall time. The resulting day string can be off by one day depending on the server TZ, causing overrides to be matched to the wrong date (slots wrongly allowed/blocked). Use explicit `dayjs.utc(...)`/`.tz(organizerTimeZone)` conversions instead.

New test does not exercise the behaviour the PR fixes

The added assertion calls getSchedule with `Asia/Dhaka` and expects exactly the same UTC slots as the `Asia/Kolkata` call, so it would also pass with the old (broken) override handling — it asserts nothing timezone-specific. Also, the PR's main claim (date overrides of fixed hosts being respected for ROUND_ROBIN events) has no test at all; a round-robin scenario with a fixed host override should be added.

Override timezone may be undefined and minute-of-day conversion drops day wrap

`dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone)` is called with `timeZone` typed optional (`TimeRange.timeZone?`); when it is undefined dayjs falls back to the local/system timezone, silently producing a wrong organizer offset. Additionally start/end are reduced to `hour()*60 + minute()` after applying the offset, so when the offset pushes the range across midnight (e.g. organizer 22:00-23:00 viewed from a +6h invitee tz) the computed endTime becomes smaller than startTime and the override yields no slots at all instead of the correct range.

Spread order can overwrite the injected userId on date overrides

`{ userId: availability.user.id, timeZone: availability.timeZone, ...override }` spreads the override last, so if an override object carries its own `userId` (the `TimeRange` type declares `userId?: number | null`) it overwrites the intended user id, breaking the per-user override matching in `getSlots`. Put the explicit fields after the spread.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unguarded access to integration.metadata['sender']['login'] can raise KeyError

`integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` is indexed directly. The `sender` key is only populated in `build_integration` when `state.get("sender")` is truthy (i.e. set by the installation webhook); for integrations created before this change, or when the webhook has not been received/processed yet, the key is absent and this raises KeyError, producing a 500 instead of the intended error page. Use `.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and treat a missing value as a verification failure.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing
OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

false_positives.candidate:
State comparison is not constant-time

`request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature` compares a user-supplied value against the pipeline signature (a secret-derived HMAC) with a non-constant-time `!=`. Since this value is now the sole CSRF/authenticity guard for the OAuth callback, prefer `hmac.compare_digest` to avoid timing-based signature discovery.

get_user_info result assumed to be a dict

`get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` result is immediately checked with `"login" not in authenticated_user_info`. If the call raises (ApiError on 401/5xx from GitHub) or returns None, this either propagates an exception or raises TypeError, resulting in a 500 during installation instead of the graceful error page. Guard the call with try/except and a None check.

safe_urlopen call for token exchange is not error-handled

`safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` is outside the try/except that only wraps `safe_urlread`/parsing. A network failure, timeout, or non-2xx handling inside safe_urlopen raises, so a transient GitHub outage during installation yields an unhandled 500 rather than the intended user-facing "invalid installation request" page. Wrap the request in the same try/except.

test_installation_not_found no longer tests the 404 installation path

The test passes `state=ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`, which does not match the pipeline signature used elsewhere (`9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`), so the request now fails at the new state-mismatch check in `OAuthLoginView` and the assertion `b"Invalid installation request."` passes without ever reaching `get_installation_info`. The previously covered behaviour ("The GitHub installation could not be found." when GitHub returns 404 for the installation) is now untested; the 404 branch in `build_integration` has no coverage.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Mutable/eager default for `queued` evaluated once at import time

`queued: datetime = timezone.now()` evaluates `timezone.now()` a single time when the module is imported, so every `AssignmentSource` instance created during the process lifetime shares the same (stale) timestamp instead of the time it was actually created. This makes the field useless for any staleness/dedup logic later on and is misleading in logs. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.

true_positives.golden_comment: to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
AssignmentSource.to_dict() puts a datetime into Celery task kwargs

`assignment_source.to_dict()` returns a dict containing a `datetime` under `queued`, and this dict is passed as a Celery task kwarg via `apply_async`. With a JSON task serializer this will fail to serialize (or be coerced to a string), which would either drop the whole outbound sync task or, on the consumer side, make `AssignmentSource.from_dict` construct an object whose `queued` is a `str` rather than a `datetime` with no type error raised. Serialize `queued` explicitly (e.g. isoformat) and parse it back in `from_dict`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.

false_positives.candidate:
New `assignment_source` kwarg passed to all sync_assignee_outbound implementations

The task now always calls `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(..., assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source)`. Any existing integration implementation of `sync_assignee_outbound` that does not accept `**kwargs` (or this keyword) will raise `TypeError` at runtime, breaking outbound assignee sync for that provider. This path is only covered by the ExampleIntegration in tests, so a non-conforming provider would not be caught. Verify/update every implementation, or pass the kwarg defensively.

from_dict does not validate/convert field types

`from_dict` just forwards the dict into the dataclass constructor, so it will happily produce an `AssignmentSource` with `integration_id` as a string or `queued` as a string (dataclasses do not enforce annotations). A string `integration_id` coming back from a serialized task payload would never equal `org_integration.integration_id` in `should_sync`, silently defeating the loop-prevention this PR adds. Coerce/validate types here.

where_should_sync still calls should_sync without a sync source

`where_should_sync` invokes `installation.should_sync(key)` with no `sync_source`, so inbound-status sync paths (`sync_status_inbound`) and the inbound-assignee lookup can still fan out to the originating integration. The new cycle-prevention only covers the outbound-assignee task; if status sync is also triggered by the same webhook, the loop remains possible. Consider threading the assignment source through here as well.

true_positives.golden_comment: MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits from StatefulDetectorHandler but only contains pass, failing to implement its required abstract methods: counter_names (property), get_dedupe_value(), get_group_key_values(), and build_occurrence_and_event_data(). This will cause a TypeError at runtime when the class is instantiated.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is False for spawn-context processes

`self.mp_context.Process` with the "spawn" context creates `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`, which derives from `BaseProcess`, not from `multiprocessing.Process` (= `multiprocessing.context.Process`). Therefore `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is False and neither `process.kill()` in `_ensure_processes_alive` nor `process.terminate()` in `join` is ever executed. Hung flusher processes are never killed before a replacement is spawned, so two processes can flush the same shards concurrently (duplicate segment production), and processes are not terminated on shutdown. Check `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess)` or `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)` instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Dead method `_create_process_for_shard`

`_create_process_for_shard(shard)` is never called anywhere after the refactor (restart now goes through `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)`). Dead code that duplicates restart logic and will silently rot / be misused; remove it.

New flusher test asserts only counts, and leaks the strategy factory pool

`test_flusher_processes_limit` checks process counts and that the total number of mapped shards is 4, but never asserts the shard->process mapping is a disjoint partition of the assigned shards (the real correctness property: no shard flushed by two processes, none dropped). It also never calls `fac.shutdown()`, leaving flusher threads/buffers around after the test.

Parent process creates one extra SpansBuffer (and Redis connections) per flusher process

`_create_process_for_shards` constructs a `SpansBuffer` in the parent and keeps it in `self.buffers`, in addition to the one pickled into the child. On every process restart a new buffer replaces the old entry without closing it, leaking Redis connections in the long-running consumer. false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.

false_positives.candidate:
Arroyo commit callback invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs in its own thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which is arroyo's `commit` callback passed to `create_with_partitions`. That callback (and the underlying consumer offset staging) is expected to be invoked from the main processing thread; calling it concurrently with the StreamProcessor's `poll`/`submit`/commit handling is not thread-safe and can corrupt or lose staged offsets. Offsets should be collected by the worker threads and flushed from `poll()` on the main thread instead.

Decode/grouping failures mark the offset complete and are silently dropped

In `submit()`, any exception from the decoder or `grouping_fn` is caught, logged, and the offset is immediately added+completed, i.e. the message is committed as if processed. There is no DLQ handling and no metric, so malformed or unexpected payloads are permanently lost with only a log line. Consider routing these to the DLQ (raise `InvalidMessage`) or at least emitting a counter.

Flaky assertion that 20 groups hit all 3 queues

`test_different_groups_distributed` asserts `len(queue_indices) == 3` based on `hash()` of 20 group keys, which is randomized per process. It is likely but not guaranteed that all three queues are hit, so this test can fail intermittently. Assert `>= 2` or seed a deterministic hash.

Per-partition lock map and defaultdicts mutated without a global lock

`_get_partition_lock` and the `defaultdict` accesses in `add_offset`/`get_committable_offsets` mutate `self.partition_locks`, `self.all_offsets` and `self.outstanding` from multiple worker threads plus the commit thread with no guarding lock (the per-partition lock is acquired only after the dict lookup/creation). This relies entirely on CPython dict/`setdefault` atomicity and will break under free-threaded builds or if the implementation changes. A single mutex guarding the maps (or a lock around lock-creation) would make the invariants explicit.

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure despite the docstring

`FixedQueuePool.__init__` creates `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, and `submit()` never raises `MessageRejected`. The class docstring for `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but nothing ever blocks or rejects: if a worker is slow, the consumer keeps reading from Kafka and buffering decoded results in memory without bound, which can OOM the consumer and also inflates offset-tracking state. A bounded queue plus raising `MessageRejected` (or blocking put) is needed to get the advertised backpressure.

WorkItem retains full Kafka message for no reason

`WorkItem.message` stores the entire arroyo `Message` (including the raw payload bytes) but is never read anywhere; partition/offset are tracked separately. With unbounded queues this doubles the memory held per queued item. Drop the field.

close() does not flush remaining committable offsets or drain queues

`close()` sets `shutdown_event`, joins the commit thread and shuts the pool down. The commit loop exits as soon as the event is set, so any work completed in the last interval (and any work the workers finish during their 5s join) is never committed. Queued-but-unprocessed items are also dropped by `queue.shutdown(immediate=False)`? they are drained only if workers keep up within the join timeout. On every consumer shutdown/rebalance this causes re-delivery (duplicate processing) of up to a second's worth of already-processed results, and silently dropped work if workers don't finish. A final `get_committable_offsets()`/commit after draining is needed.

hash() of group key is not stable across processes

`get_queue_for_group` uses builtin `hash(group_key)`, which for `str` is salted per process (PYTHONHASHSEED). The docstring claims "consistent hashing", but assignment differs between consumer processes and across restarts. This is tolerable since each process owns distinct partitions, but if ordering guarantees are ever expected to hold across processes/restarts this is wrong; use a stable hash (e.g. md5/crc32) instead.

join() ignores its timeout argument

`join(timeout)` discards `timeout` and calls `close()`, which uses hard-coded 5s joins for the commit thread and each worker. With N queues this can block for N*5s during shutdown, exceeding arroyo's join timeout and triggering a forced kill mid-processing. The timeout should be honoured/budgeted across the threads.

queue.ShutDown / Queue.shutdown require Python 3.13+

`queue.ShutDown` and `queue.Queue.shutdown(immediate=...)` were only added in Python 3.13. On any older interpreter this module raises `AttributeError` at worker-exception handling time and `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` logs "Error shutting down queue" for every queue while workers stay blocked in `get()` forever, so the consumer can never shut down. If the runtime is not guaranteed to be 3.13+, this needs a compatibility path (e.g. sentinel items).

queue_pool is created once per factory and destroyed by strategy close(), breaking rebalances

The `FixedQueuePool` (and its worker threads and `OffsetTracker`) is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__`, but `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`terminate()` call `queue_pool.shutdown()`, which stops all worker threads and shuts down the queues. Arroyo calls `create_with_partitions` again after every rebalance/partition revocation. On the second call, `assert self.queue_pool is not None` still passes (the attribute isn't cleared by the strategy), so a new strategy is built on top of dead workers and already-shutdown queues: submitted work is never processed and offsets are never committed, stalling the consumer silently. Additionally the `OffsetTracker`'s `last_committed`/`all_offsets` are carried across assignments, so stale per-partition state can suppress commits (or commit offsets for partitions no longer owned) after a rebalance. The pool should be created per `create_with_partitions` call (or reset on revocation).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

false_positives.candidate:
Cached denials are not invalidated when permissions are granted

Check now stores a positive deny entry (permDenialCache, shortCacheTTL=30s) for every (namespace, user, action, name, parent) that is denied after a DB query, and returns early on a hit without consulting the DB. There is no invalidation path when a permission is subsequently granted (e.g. a user is given access to an existing dashboard/folder immediately after being denied), so the user will keep receiving 403s for up to 30 seconds even though the fresh DB state allows access. This is the inverse of the problem the PR fixes; consider a shorter TTL or an invalidation hook.

Denial cache key omits identity type, risking cross-identity collisions

userPermDenialCacheKey is built from namespace, userUID, action, name and parent only. Subjects of different identity types can share the same UID string (e.g. `user:0`, `anonymous:0`, `render:0`, or a service account whose UID equals a user UID), so a denial recorded for one identity can be returned as a cached deny for a different identity in Check (service.go:116-121). Unlike permCache, which uses distinct key builders per identity type (anonymousPermCacheKey vs userPermCacheKey), the denial key has no type discriminator. This produces incorrect authz decisions (wrongful denials, and incorrect caching semantics). Include the identity type in the key.

Non-ErrNotFound errors from getCachedIdentityPermissions are silently ignored

getCachedIdentityPermissions can return real errors (e.g. GetUserIdentifiers store failure, or 'unsupported identity type'). In Check (line 123) and List (line 180) any error is treated the same as a cache miss, so genuine backend failures are swallowed and the code proceeds to a second lookup; the error cause is lost from logs/traces. Distinguish cache.ErrNotFound from other errors.

Per-resource denial cache entries can grow unboundedly

The denial cache key includes the resource name and parent folder, so every distinct denied resource for every user creates a separate entry in the shared local cache. In workloads where many checks are denied (e.g. scanning/listing a large number of dashboards per user), this produces a very large number of cache entries with no bound other than the 30s TTL and 2–10 min cleanup interval, increasing memory pressure on the shared cache that also holds permissions, teams and folder trees.

cacheHit test field is now dead and cached-permission path untested in getUserPermissions

The 'should return permissions from cache if available' case was removed from TestService_getUserPermissions, leaving the cacheHit field always false and the `if tc.cacheHit` branches (lines 367-369, 388-392) unreachable. Since getUserPermissions no longer reads permCache, there is no test asserting that it always re-queries the store (the behaviour change this PR relies on), nor that the permission cache is still written. Add an explicit assertion that the store is queried even when permCache is populated.

permissionCacheUsage metric double-counted / wrongly labelled in Check

In Check, a denial-cache hit increments permissionCacheUsage with label "true" and returns; on a permission-cache hit that results in allow it also increments "true"; but on a permission-cache hit that results in deny the code falls through and increments "false" at line 137 even though the cache was hit. The metric therefore no longer reflects cache hit ratio and mixes denial-cache hits with permission-cache hits, making it unusable for tuning.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
Assertion on interpolation call count codifies the double-interpolation behaviour

The test was changed from expecting interpolation once to `expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)`. That number is exactly 1 (shard splitting) + 4 (re-interpolation inside runSplitQuery per sub-request), i.e. the test now locks in the duplicate interpolation described above instead of verifying that each query is interpolated exactly once. If the duplication is fixed this assertion must change; as written it hides the defect.

Queries are interpolated twice when shard splitting delegates to runSplitQuery

runShardSplitQuery now applies datasource.applyTemplateVariables to each target, and the resulting sub-request is handed to runSplitQuery (line 163), which in querySplitting.ts (line 299) applies applyTemplateVariables again to every target. Every shard sub-request therefore goes through template/ad-hoc-filter interpolation twice (the updated test even asserts applyTemplateVariables is called 5 times for a single query). This can duplicate ad-hoc filters / label filters injected by applyTemplateVariables, re-interpolate values that themselves contain `$`-like text, and recompute `$__auto`/step against the already-substituted expression, producing incorrect queries. One of the two interpolation points should be removed (e.g. let runSplitQuery skip interpolation when called from shard splitting).

runSplitQuery may re-interpolate already-interpolated targets from other callers

runSplitQuery unconditionally calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables on request.targets. Callers that already interpolate before calling runSplitQuery (shard splitting, and any datasource.query path that pre-processes targets) will now have variables/ad-hoc filters applied a second time. There is no guard or flag to opt out, so the function's contract silently changed: passing pre-interpolated targets is no longer safe. Consider adding an option (e.g. `skipInterpolation`) or documenting/enforcing that callers must pass raw targets.

false_positives.candidate:

Logger interface extended with FromContext (breaking for implementers)

Adding FromContext(context.Context) Logger to the exported plugins/log.Logger interface breaks any existing implementation of that interface outside this package (e.g. in enterprise or test helpers), which will no longer compile. SubscribeStream, PublishStream and RunStream pass the context through without calling instrumentContext, so logs emitted during stream handling (and by LoggerMiddleware for these endpoints) carry no pluginId/endpoint/dsUID attributes. true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Count-then-insert is not atomic, limit can be exceeded

CreateOrUpdateDevice reads the device count and then inserts in a separate statement/session. Concurrent anonymous requests (or multiple Grafana instances sharing the DB) can all observe count < deviceLimit and each insert, so the stored device count can exceed the configured device_limit. A transaction with appropriate locking, or an atomic INSERT ... SELECT guarded by the count, is needed if the limit is meant to be enforced.

true_positives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device tagging moved onto the request path adds a DB count+write per anonymous request

TagDevice was previously executed in a background goroutine with its own timeout; it is now called synchronously inside Authenticate. For every anonymous request that misses the local cache this now performs a SELECT COUNT(*) on anon_device plus an upsert before the request can proceed, and any DB latency/failure directly affects anonymous page loads. Under high anonymous traffic with a configured limit this COUNT query over a large table is a notable added cost.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
rowsAffected==0 wrongly treated as device limit reached on MySQL / unchanged rows

updateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached whenever the UPDATE affects 0 rows. With MySQL (default CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS off) an UPDATE that matches an existing row but sets identical values reports 0 affected rows, so an already-registered anonymous device whose client_ip/user_agent/updated_at are unchanged would be denied authentication even though it is within the limit. The error is also semantically wrong for the 'device not found' case; a known device should succeed. Consider checking existence explicitly (SELECT) instead of relying on rows affected.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
localCache is populated before the store write, letting over-limit devices bypass the limit

tagDeviceUI calls a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{}) before CreateOrUpdateDevice. If the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached (and the request is therefore rejected in Anonymous.Authenticate), the device id is nevertheless cached, so for the next ~29 minutes tagDeviceUI returns nil early and the same unknown device is granted anonymous access without ever being recorded. The limit is effectively bypassed by retrying. The cache should only be set after a successful write.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Device limit tests do not cover the update path for an existing device at the limit

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only asserts that a *new* device id is rejected once the limit is hit. There is no test that an already-registered device still succeeds (updates its updated_at/client_ip) when the limit is reached — exactly the path that is broken by the rowsAffected==0 logic on MySQL/unchanged rows. Add a case re-tagging the existing device id after the limit is reached.

New auth.anonymous device_limit option not documented in defaults.ini/sample.ini or docs

cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit is read from [auth.anonymous] device_limit, but no entry was added to conf/defaults.ini, conf/sample.ini, or the configuration docs. Users have no discoverable way to learn about the setting or its default (0 = unlimited), and Grafana convention is that every ini option is listed in defaults.ini.
