ProvideAnonDBStore now takes an extra int64 argument and AnonDeviceService constructs the store itself instead of receiving anonstore.AnonStore. If ProvideAnonDBStore is still registered as a provider in pkg/server/wire.go (not included in this PR), wire will fail to build because there is no provider for int64, and any other consumer of the injected AnonStore loses it. Verify the DI graph was updated.

Raw ErrDeviceLimitReached returned from Authenticate yields an unhelpful 500/opaque error

ErrDeviceLimitReached is created with fmt.Errorf and returned directly from Authenticate. The authn layer expects typed errutil errors to produce a correct HTTP status and user-facing message; a plain error will surface as a generic internal error rather than a clear 'anonymous device limit reached' response, and gives no way for the frontend to show the limit message implied by the new anonymousDeviceLimit frontend setting.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Debug logging left in at Error level, logging full ID lists

`r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", ..., "ids", ids, ...)` (and the analogous calls at lines 537, 554, 557, 576, 579) log routine, successful cleanup progress at ERROR severity, and include the entire batch of IDs. With a batch size of up to tens of thousands this produces huge log lines every cleanup cycle and will trigger error alerting/noise for operators. These should be removed or downgraded to Debug without dumping the ID slice.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup job ticker reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute

The background cleanup ticker was changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This makes all cleanup jobs (temp files, snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, query history) run 10x more often, which is a significant and unrelated behavior/load change — and because each `clean()` run has a 9-minute timeout, runs can now overlap/stack up. This looks like leftover debugging from testing the annotation cleanup and should be reverted.

false_positives.candidate:
SQLite parameter-limit check uses configured batch size instead of actual ID count

The decision whether to inline IDs into the DELETE statement is based on `r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > sqliteParameterLimit` rather than `len(ids) > sqliteParameterLimit`. Also, the limit is applied only for SQLite; other drivers have their own limits (e.g. Postgres allows at most 65535 bind parameters), so a batch size above that would fail at runtime on Postgres. Basing the branch on `len(ids)` and applying a safe limit for all backends (or chunking the deletes) would be more robust.

fetchIDs builds SQL by string concatenation of caller-provided condition

`fetchIDs` interpolates both the table name and a free-form `condition` string directly into the SQL text, and callers build the condition with `fmt.Sprintf` including `annotationType` and `cutoffDate`. Current callers pass constants/ints so there is no live injection, but this pattern is fragile: any future caller passing user-derived input creates an injection. Parameterizing the cutoff date and keeping the condition to a fixed set of templates would avoid this.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete puts the un-enriched logger in the context

`ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` uses the base logger rather than `log`, so downstream code logging from the context loses the name/kind/method values that every other method in this file propagates.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
DeleteCollection legacy goroutine records storage duration

The goroutine measuring the legacy DeleteCollection calls `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` instead of `recordLegacyDuration`, so legacy delete-collection latency/errors are never recorded and storage metrics are double-counted with legacy timings.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete success passes object name as the 'kind' metric label

`d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the resource name instead of `options.Kind`. Since the name is unbounded per-object, this creates an unbounded-cardinality Prometheus label, risking memory blowup in the metrics registry, and makes the metric unusable for per-kind aggregation.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit request context and get cancelled

All four goroutines (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163) build their timeout context from the incoming request ctx (`context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`). The apiserver cancels the request context as soon as the HTTP handler returns, which typically happens before the goroutine completes. The legacy write will then fail with context canceled, silently dropping the legacy copy that mode 3 exists to maintain. Use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (preserving auth/user values) as the parent before applying the timeout.

Legacy Update receives the raw objInfo, re-applying the patch against the legacy object

The previous implementation wrapped objInfo with the already-updated object (`updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}`) before calling legacy. Now the raw `objInfo` is passed, so legacy will call `UpdatedObject` against its own stored object. For patch/apply requests this can produce a different result than what was written to unified storage (and resourceVersion precondition checks are evaluated against legacy's RV), causing the two stores to diverge or the legacy update to fail with a conflict.

Local registry shadows package-level one inconsistently

`p := prometheus.NewRegistry()` inside TestMode3_Get shadows the package-level `p` used by every other test here, while the mode1 test removed exactly this pattern. All other subtests reuse one global registry across many NewDualWriter calls; if the metrics registration uses MustRegister this repeated registration of the same collectors will panic. Pick one approach (fresh registry per test is safest) and apply it consistently.

Storage error path records legacy duration metric

In Create, when `d.Storage.Create` fails the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` even though the failing call was to unified storage. Same in Update (line 129). This mislabels failures: storage error rates/latencies will be missing and legacy metrics will be polluted with storage failures. Should be `recordStorageDuration`.

Tests never synchronize with the async legacy write

Mode 3 now performs the legacy write in a goroutine, but the tests return immediately after the storage call. Nothing asserts that Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection is invoked, so the core behaviour of this PR is untested. Worse, the shared `mock.Mock` is read/written by the goroutine after the test function finishes, which is a data race (will fail under -race) and can cause 'mock called after test completion' panics. Add a synchronization hook (e.g. a channel/WaitGroup signalled from the mock's Run function) and assert the legacy calls.

Unrelated and duplicated go.work.sum entries

This PR adds ~16 go.work.sum lines unrelated to the dual-writer change, including a duplicate `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod` entry that already exists two lines above. These look like accidental local-tooling churn and should be dropped from the PR.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No re-check of cache after acquiring write lock

After taking the write lock the function does not re-verify that entryPointAssetsCache is still nil. Concurrent cold-start requests will each serialize on the mutex and redundantly parse/fetch the manifest (including an HTTP request in the CDN case) even though an earlier goroutine already populated the cache.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache overwritten with nil on read failure

When readWebAssetsFromFile/CDN fails, result is nil and it is still assigned to entryPointAssetsCache, clobbering a previously good cached value and forcing every subsequent request to re-read the manifest (and return nil). Guard the assignment with `if result != nil` / `err == nil`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions is dead logic that unconditionally returns false

`enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns `false` in both branches, so the feature-flag read has no effect and the variable is pointless. The function is effectively `return false`. This is confusing (a reader could think the flag re-enables the feature, and the inverted `!` suggests the opposite of the intent) and is prone to breaking if someone 'fixes' the branch later. Replace with an explicit unconditional rejection (or a correctly polarised flag check) and drop the unused feature lookup.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Stub DB silently keeps SQL expression code path alive with runtime errors

The new stub `sql.DB` returns "not implemented" from `TablesList`, `RunCommands` and `QueryFramesInto`. In `SQLCommand.Execute` (pkg/expr/sql_command.go:100) this error is placed into `rsp.Error` and `nil` is returned, so the legacy (non-reader) SQL expression path returns a generic opaque "not implemented" to the user instead of a clear 'feature disabled' message. Consider short-circuiting in `NewSQLCommand`/`UnmarshalSQLCommand` with an explicit disabled error so behaviour is consistent across both entry points.

false_positives.candidate:
No test asserting SQL expressions are rejected

This change is a security fix disabling the SQL expression query type, but no test was added verifying that `ReadQuery` with `QueryTypeSQL` returns an error (both with and without the `sqlExpressions` feature flag enabled), nor that `UnmarshalSQLCommand`/`SQLCommand.Execute` no longer executes SQL. Without such a test, a future change to `enableSqlExpressions` could silently reintroduce CVE-2024-9264.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the write lock around BuildIndex allows concurrent builds for the same key

BuildIndex previously held b.cacheMu for the whole function, serializing all index builds. Now only the final cache write is locked. Two concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same NamespacedResource (e.g. a watch event triggering getOrCreateIndex while the startup indexing is still building, or two concurrent searches for the same key) will both call bleve.New on the same directory path (b.opts.Root/namespace/resource.group). bleve.New fails if the path already exists, so the second build errors out; for the mem-only case both builds complete and one index is silently discarded while duplicating all the indexing work and double-counting the IndexTenants metric. Consider per-key locking (e.g. an in-flight map or singleflight) rather than dropping the lock entirely.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs reads b.cache without holding cacheMu

TotalDocs iterates b.cache with no lock while BuildIndex now writes to the map under b.cacheMu. Previously builds held the lock for their whole duration, which reduced the window; with the finer-grained locking, concurrent builds (startup indexing workers, watch-event driven builds) can write to the map while TotalDocs ranges over it, which is an unsynchronized map read/write and will trigger a fatal 'concurrent map iteration and map write' panic. TotalDocs is called from searchSupport.init logging, so this is reachable. Take b.cacheMu.RLock() in TotalDocs.

false_positives.candidate:
NewResourceServer leaks the server context and background goroutines when Init fails

s.Init(ctx) is now called in the constructor, but on error the function returns nil without calling the cancel func created at line 229. Any goroutines already started by the search watcher (searchSupport.init starts a watch goroutine on context.Background()) and by the backend poller keep running, and the cancelable context is never released. Call cancel() (and ideally s.Stop) before returning the error.

Postgres path of the storage-server integration test is skipped without a tracking issue

The only integration coverage for running the storage server target with Postgres is now unconditionally skipped with a 'works locally' comment. Since this PR changes when unified storage initialization happens (now during server construction), this is exactly the path that would catch startup regressions on Postgres. At minimum reference a tracking issue so the skip does not become permanent.

Shared err and counter written from concurrent errgroup goroutines

Inside the errgroup in searchSupport.init, each goroutine assigns to the enclosing `err` variable (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and increments the shared `totalBatchesIndexed` counter. With initWorkers > 1 these are unsynchronized writes from multiple goroutines: a data race, and `err` is also read after group.Wait() (line 195), so a failure in one namespace can be masked or an unrelated error reported. Use a goroutine-local `err :=` and an atomic/locked counter.

Stop() no longer has any effect on request handling since Init checks were removed

Stop sets s.initErr to 'service is stopping'/'service is stopped' as a guard, but every request handler's `if err := s.Init(ctx)` check was removed in this PR. After Stop, Create/Update/Delete/Read/List/Watch/Search/blob calls will proceed against a cancelled context and a stopped backend instead of returning a clear 'service is stopped' error. Either add an explicit stopped/served state check in the handlers or drop the now-dead initErr mutation in Stop.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Test cleanup registers the literal alias "alias" so created IDPs are never removed

`getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)` uses the hard-coded string "alias" rather than the created provider's alias (`idp-alias-N`). None of the 21 identity providers created by testCacheIDPForLogin are deleted after the test, and the cleanup call itself will fail/404. This leaks state into other tests in the realm (same bug is repeated at lines 303 and 425).

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
getForLogin cache is not invalidated on organization changes

Unlike getByOrganization (line 173), which checks `isInvalid(orgId)` in addition to its own cache key, getForLogin only checks `isInvalid(cacheKey)`. Removing/disabling an organization, or changing an organization's identity-provider membership through the organization provider (which invalidates the organization id, not the `.idp.login.*` keys), will leave the ORG_ONLY/ALL login caches populated with stale IDP id sets. Consumers that call getForLogin and don't re-check `isEnabled()` (the wrapper only hides disabled orgs, not removed org links) will see providers that should no longer be offered for login. Consider also checking `isInvalid(organizationId)` and registering login-cache invalidations in the organization provider.

getLoginPredicate semantics changed for org-linked IDPs

`getLoginPredicate()` now additionally rejects any IDP that has an organizationId unless its config has BROKER_PUBLIC=true. This is a public SPI helper that may be used by callers other than the new invalidation logic (e.g. bean/federated-provider filtering); for them, non-public organization brokers will silently disappear from results. If the restriction is only needed for cache invalidation, it should be a separate predicate, or the behavior change should be documented in the method javadoc.

remove() always issues an extra DB lookup by alias

`idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias)` is now executed unconditionally in `remove()`, even when the entry is present (and valid) in the cache, where previously the cached model was used. This adds a database round-trip to every IDP removal. The stored model could be obtained from the cached entry in the else-branch instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default KeyStore provider

The method is documented to return a BouncyCastle (FIPS or non-FIPS) security provider, but here it returns whatever JCA provider supplies the default KeyStore type. Callers such as `BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER` will then pass e.g. "SUN" as a provider name to algorithm lookups, which can fail with NoSuchProviderException for algorithms that provider doesn't implement. Returning null or throwing UnsupportedOperationException (consistent with the other unsupported methods) would be clearer than returning an unrelated provider.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead/duplicated ASN1 encoding calls

Lines 114-115 create two ASN1Encoder instances, write r and s, and discard the results; the actual DER is built again on lines 117-121. These two statements are dead code (wasted allocation and confusing); they should be removed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract method order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

`int order()` is added to the public `CryptoProvider` interface without a `default` implementation. Any third-party or downstream (e.g. keycloak-client repo, custom FIPS integrations) implementation of this interface will fail to compile / throw AbstractMethodError at runtime after upgrade. Give it a `default int order() { return 100; }` (or similar) to keep binary/source compatibility.

false_negatives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
Test uses a default (P-256) EC key for ES384/ES512, so it does not verify real conversions

`KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` uses the default curve (usually secp256r1) for all three tests. For ES384/ES512 the signature produced is a P-256 signature, while `algorithm.getSignatureLength()` is 96/132, so `asn1derToConcatenatedRS` silently zero-pads and the round-trip assertion passes without exercising correct ES384/ES512 behaviour. Generate the matching curve per algorithm (secp256r1/secp384r1/secp521r1) and also assert that the re-derived DER signature verifies with `Signature.verify`, so a real encoding bug would be caught.

Ties in provider order are resolved non-deterministically instead of failing

Previously, finding more than one CryptoProvider on the classpath threw IllegalStateException. Now providers are only sorted by `order()`, and DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider and WildFlyElytronProvider all return 200. If two of these end up on the classpath (a realistic misconfiguration, e.g. FIPS + default BC), the selection depends on ServiceLoader/sort stability and the server may silently run with the wrong crypto provider (e.g. non-FIPS BC in FIPS mode) instead of failing fast. Consider throwing when the top two providers have equal order, or at least logging at WARN.

logger.debugf called with dynamic string as format

`logger.debugf(builder.toString())` passes a runtime-built message as a format string with no arguments. Any '%' character in a provider class name (or future message content) would cause an UnknownFormatConversionException inside logging. Use `logger.debug(builder.toString())` or `logger.debugf("%s", ...)`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup listener now skipped when only V2 is enabled

The removal listener (role/client/group removal -> setPermissionsEnabled(false)) is now guarded by Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ. If a deployment previously created V1 permission resources and then runs with ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ disabled (e.g. only V2 enabled), orphan authorization resources/policies for removed roles, clients and groups will no longer be cleaned up, leaving stale data. Consider still cleaning up V1 data regardless of the flag, or document the migration.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission can return the resource-type resource name

resourceStore.findByType(server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...) also matches the generic 'Clients' resource created by the schema for all-clients permissions (its type equals the resource type). Its name ('Clients') is not a client id, so the returned set may contain a bogus entry that callers use to filter/lookup clients, leading to incorrect client listings. Skip the resource whose name equals CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE (or expand it to all clients).

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Possible NPE when the 'Clients' resource-type resource is missing

In hasPermission(ClientModel, String), when no per-client resource exists the code falls back to AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(...), which can return null (it returns null when the realm doesn't support the authz schema, when the type is unknown, or when the named resource simply isn't found). The returned value is passed directly to policyStore.findByResource(server, resource) and then dereferenced via resource.getScopes(), so a null fallback causes a NullPointerException (HTTP 500) instead of a clean 'deny'. Add a null check returning false.

true_positives.golden_comment: Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead code and unused imports in new class

getEvaluationContext(...) is private and never used, and the imports for TOKEN_EXCHANGE, Scope, ClientModelIdentity, DefaultEvaluationContext, EvaluationContext and the unused `logger` field are dead. Removing them avoids confusion about token-exchange evaluation being supported in V2 (canExchangeTo throws UnsupportedOperationException).

false_negatives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

false_positives.candidate:
getResourceName not implemented for the new Clients resource type

getResourceName() only handles the USERS resource type; for policies with resourceType 'Clients' it falls through to resource.getDisplayName(), which is not set for resources created by getOrCreateResource(). As a result the admin API/console will show null/empty names for client-scoped permissions instead of the clientId (and 'All clients' for the type resource). Add a CLIENTS branch resolving the client by id.

true_positives.golden_comment: Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Exit code 4 changed meaning: was 'recreate required', now 'feature disabled'

RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE was changed from 4 to 3 and 4 is now reused for FEATURE_DISABLED. Any existing automation/pipeline written against the previously released behaviour that treats exit code 4 as 'recreate upgrade required' will now silently interpret a 'feature not enabled' failure as a recreate signal (and vice versa, a real recreate requirement returns 3 which such scripts likely treat as unexpected). If backwards compatibility matters, pick an unused code (e.g. 5) for FEATURE_DISABLED instead of recycling 4, and call out the change in the release notes.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:

false_positives.candidate:
Feature-disabled path only tested for 'metadata', exit code not asserted

testFeatureNotEnabled only exercises the `metadata` subcommand and asserts the error text; it does not assert the new exit code (CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED) nor cover the `check` subcommand, which has the same new guard. Since the documented contract is the exit code (docs/guides/server/update-compatibility.adoc lists code 4), a regression in the exit code or in the `check` guard would go unnoticed.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
canManage() for all groups is granted by the VIEW scope

GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() (the no-argument variant used by GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup via requireManage()) evaluates `hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE)`. This means an admin who only has the `view` scope on the `Groups` resource type is allowed to create top-level groups (and anything else gated by canManage()). The scope list should only contain MANAGE, as canManage(GroupModel) correctly does.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns resource IDs and evaluates permissions with the wrong key

For FGAP v2 the group resource is created with `name` = group id (AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup) and a separate generated resource `id`. Here the code (a) calls `hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...)`, but hasPermission looks the resource up with `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)`, so it never finds the per-group resource and always falls back to the "all groups" resource; and (b) adds `groupResource.getId()` to the returned set, while callers (UsersResource.searchForUser via session attribute UserModel.GROUPS, and UsersResource.getUsersCount) expect group IDs. Consequently per-group view-members permissions are ignored by this method and, when a result is returned, user searches/counts are filtered by non-existent group IDs. Use `groupResource.getName()` for both the permission lookup and the returned set.

false_positives.candidate:
Group removal listener will fail with UnsupportedOperationException when FGAP v2 is enabled

AdminPermissions.registerListener (registered when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ is enabled) handles GroupModel.GroupRemovedEvent by calling `management(session, realm).groups().setPermissionsEnabled(group, false)`. With ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 also enabled, `management()` returns MgmtPermissionsV2, whose new `groups()` override returns GroupPermissionsV2, which throws UnsupportedOperationException from setPermissionsEnabled. Deleting any group (and GroupResource#getManagementPermissions / setManagementPermissionsEnabled, which call isPermissionsEnabled/getPermissions) will therefore fail with a 500 when both features are on.

Javadoc on requireManageMembers refers to the wrong method

The Javadoc of `requireManageMembers(GroupModel)` states it throws ForbiddenException if `canManageMembership(GroupModel)` returns false; it actually checks `canManageMembers(GroupModel)`. This is misleading for implementers of the interface. Also, `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission` is documented as returning a "Stream of IDs" while it returns a Set.

Possible NPE when the "Groups" resource-type resource is absent

`AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceTypeResource` returns null if the schema is not supported for the resource server or the resource is not found. The returned value is used immediately in `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource)` and `resource.getScopes()` without a null check, which would throw a NullPointerException (HTTP 500) instead of simply denying access. Add a null guard returning false.

getResourceName does not resolve group names for the new Groups resource type

Now that GROUPS is part of the schema, policies of resource type `Groups` store the group id as the resource name. getResourceName only special-cases USERS, so for group permissions it falls through to `resource.getDisplayName()`, which is null for these generated resources. The admin console/REST representation will show no (or a raw) name for group permissions. A branch resolving the group (including the "All groups" case for the resource named `Groups`) is needed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The translation is in Italian instead of Lithuanian. This should be translated to Lithuanian to match the file's locale (messages_lt.properties).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Lithuanian translation replaced with Italian text

`loginTotpStep1` was replaced with `Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:` — Italian text in a Lithuanian bundle. The `FixedQueuePool` (and its worker threads and `OffsetTracker`) is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__`, but `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`terminate()` call `queue_pool.shutdown()`, which stops all worker threads and shuts down the queues. Arroyo calls `create_with_partitions` again after every rebalance/partition revocation. On the second call, `assert self.queue_pool is not None` still passes (the attribute isn't cleared by the strategy), so a new strategy is built on top of dead workers and already-shutdown queues: submitted work is never processed and offsets are never committed, stalling the consumer silently. Additionally the `OffsetTracker`'s `last_committed`/`all_offsets` are carried across assignments, so stale per-partition state can suppress commits (or commit offsets for partitions no longer owned) after a rebalance. The pool should be created per `create_with_partitions` call (or reset on revocation).

Arroyo commit callback invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs in its own thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which is arroyo's `commit` callback passed to `create_with_partitions`. That callback (and the underlying consumer offset staging) is expected to be invoked from the main processing thread; calling it concurrently with the StreamProcessor's `poll`/`submit`/commit handling is not thread-safe and can corrupt or lose staged offsets. Offsets should be collected by the worker threads and flushed from `poll()` on the main thread instead.

close() does not flush remaining committable offsets or drain queues

`close()` sets `shutdown_event`, joins the commit thread and shuts the pool down. The commit loop exits as soon as the event is set, so any work completed in the last interval (and any work the workers finish during their 5s join) is never committed. Queued-but-unprocessed items are also dropped by `queue.shutdown(immediate=False)`? they are drained only if workers keep up within the join timeout. On every consumer shutdown/rebalance this causes re-delivery (duplicate processing) of up to a second's worth of already-processed results, and silently dropped work if workers don't finish. A final `get_committable_offsets()`/commit after draining is needed.

`queue.ShutDown` and `queue.Queue.shutdown(immediate=...)` were only added in Python 3.13. On any older interpreter this module raises `AttributeError` at worker-exception handling time and `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` logs "Error shutting down queue" for every queue while workers stay blocked in `get()` forever, so the consumer can never shut down. If the runtime is not guaranteed to be 3.13+, this needs a compatibility path (e.g. sentinel items).

Decode/grouping failures mark the offset complete and are silently dropped

In `submit()`, any exception from the decoder or `grouping_fn` is caught, logged, and the offset is immediately added+completed, i.e. the message is committed as if processed. There is no DLQ handling and no metric, so malformed or unexpected payloads are permanently lost with only a log line. Consider routing these to the DLQ (raise `InvalidMessage`) or at least emitting a counter.

Per-partition lock map and defaultdicts mutated without a global lock

`_get_partition_lock` and the `defaultdict` accesses in `add_offset`/`get_committable_offsets` mutate `self.partition_locks`, `self.all_offsets` and `self.outstanding` from multiple worker threads plus the commit thread with no guarding lock (the per-partition lock is acquired only after the dict lookup/creation). This relies entirely on CPython dict/`setdefault` atomicity and will break under free-threaded builds or if the implementation changes. A single mutex guarding the maps (or a lock around lock-creation) would make the invariants explicit.

`get_queue_for_group` uses builtin `hash(group_key)`, which for `str` is salted per process (PYTHONHASHSEED). The docstring claims "consistent hashing", but assignment differs between consumer processes and across restarts. This is tolerable since each process owns distinct partitions, but if ordering guarantees are ever expected to hold across processes/restarts this is wrong; use a stable hash (e.g. md5/crc32) instead.

`WorkItem.message` stores the entire arroyo `Message` (including the raw payload bytes) but is never read anywhere; partition/offset are tracked separately. With unbounded queues this doubles the memory held per queued item. Drop the field.

`test_different_groups_distributed` asserts `len(queue_indices) == 3` based on `hash()` of 20 group keys, which is randomized per process. It is likely but not guaranteed that all three queues are hit, so this test can fail intermittently. Assert `>= 2` or seed a deterministic hash.

`join(timeout)` discards `timeout` and calls `close()`, which uses hard-coded 5s joins for the commit thread and each worker. Denial cache key omits identity type, risking cross-identity collisions

userPermDenialCacheKey is built from namespace, userUID, action, name and parent only. Subjects of different identity types can share the same UID string (e.g. `user:0`, `anonymous:0`, `render:0`, or a service account whose UID equals a user UID), so a denial recorded for one identity can be returned as a cached deny for a different identity in Check (service.go:116-121). Unlike permCache, which uses distinct key builders per identity type (anonymousPermCacheKey vs userPermCacheKey), the denial key has no type discriminator. This produces incorrect authz decisions (wrongful denials, and incorrect caching semantics). Include the identity type in the key.

Cached denials are not invalidated when permissions are granted

There is no invalidation path when a permission is subsequently granted (e.g. a user is given access to an existing dashboard/folder immediately after being denied), so the user will keep receiving 403s for up to 30 seconds even though the fresh DB state allows access. This is the inverse of the problem the PR fixes; consider a shorter TTL or an invalidation hook.

Per-resource denial cache entries can grow unboundedly

The denial cache key includes the resource name and parent folder, so every distinct denied resource for every user creates a separate entry in the shared local cache. In workloads where many checks are denied (e.g. scanning/listing a large number of dashboards per user), this produces a very large number of cache entries with no bound other than the 30s TTL and 2–10 min cleanup interval, increasing memory pressure on the shared cache that also holds permissions, teams and folder trees.

permissionCacheUsage metric double-counted / wrongly labelled in Check

In Check, a denial-cache hit increments permissionCacheUsage with label "true" and returns; on a permission-cache hit that results in allow it also increments "true"; but on a permission-cache hit that results in deny the code falls through and increments "false" at line 137 even though the cache was hit. The metric therefore no longer reflects cache hit ratio and mixes denial-cache hits with permission-cache hits, making it unusable for tuning.

Non-ErrNotFound errors from getCachedIdentityPermissions are silently ignored

getCachedIdentityPermissions can return real errors (e.g. GetUserIdentifiers store failure, or 'unsupported identity type'). In Check (line 123) and List (line 180) any error is treated the same as a cache miss, so genuine backend failures are swallowed and the code proceeds to a second lookup; the error cause is lost from logs/traces. Distinguish cache.ErrNotFound from other errors.

cacheHit test field is now dead and cached-permission path untested in getUserPermissions

The 'should return permissions from cache if available' case was removed from TestService_getUserPermissions, leaving the cacheHit field always false and the `if tc.cacheHit` branches (lines 367-369, 388-392) unreachable. Since getUserPermissions no longer reads permCache, there is no test asserting that it always re-queries the store (the behaviour change this PR relies on), nor that the permission cache is still written. Add an explicit assertion that the store is queried even when permCache is populated.

Cancellation sweep does not filter by method and aborts all remaining cancellations on first error

`remindersToCancel` queries only `cancelled: true` without `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL`, so any non-email reminder that ever gets flagged cancelled will have its Twilio SID posted to the SendGrid `scheduled_sends` endpoint. More importantly the whole `for` loop is inside a single try/catch: if one SendGrid request fails (invalid/expired batch id, rate limit), the loop exits and every remaining reminder in this run is left uncancelled, so their emails may be sent before the next cron tick (the window is only 1 hour while the cron runs every 15 min, so a couple of failed runs is enough to leak reminders). Each reminder should be cancelled/deleted in its own try/catch and the query should be scoped to EMAIL.

The new cancellation requests (and the existing `/v3/mail/batch` call) therefore go out unauthenticated and will fail with 401, meaning cancelled reminders are never actually cancelled — the exact bug this PR is meant to fix.

Backup codes stored reversibly encrypted instead of hashed

Backup codes are persisted as `symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(codes))` (setup.ts) and compared by decrypting and `indexOf` here. They should be hashed individually (e.g. bcrypt/argon2) and compared by hash, as is done for passwords.

If `user.backupCodes` was written with a different encryption key or is otherwise corrupt, `symmetricDecrypt`/`JSON.parse` throws a raw exception that surfaces as a generic 500 rather than a meaningful ErrorCode, breaking login for that user with no diagnostic. Anchor sanitization removes the wrong occurrence and can misreport santizeAnchors() iterates matches of the translated value with `matcher`, but then does `value = value.replaceFirst(Pattern.quote(englishMatcher.group()), "")` — it mutates `value` while `matcher` still iterates over the original string, and replaceFirst always removes the *first* occurrence rather than the one just matched. For a value with several identical anchors (e.g. two ``), the wrong occurrences get stripped and the loop indices no longer line up with the mutated string, so legitimate values can be reported as illegal HTML, or illegal anchors can be silently stripped and missed. When the plugin runs over hundreds of properties files, a maintainer cannot tell which translation failed. Include `key` and `file` in the message.

Arroyo calls `create_with_partitions` again after every rebalance/partition revocation. On the second call, `assert self.queue_pool is not None` still passes (the attribute isn't cleared by the strategy), so a new strategy is built on top of dead workers and already-shutdown queues: submitted work is never processed and offsets are never committed, stalling the consumer silently. Additionally the `OffsetTracker`'s `last_committed`/`all_offsets` are carried across assignments, so stale per-partition state can suppress commits (or commit offsets for partitions no longer owned) after a rebalance. The pool should be created per `create_with_partitions` call (or reset on revocation).

Arroyo commit callback invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs in its own thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which is arroyo's `commit` callback passed to `create_with_partitions`. That callback (and the underlying consumer offset staging) is expected to be invoked from the main processing thread; calling it concurrently with the StreamProcessor's `poll`/`submit`/commit handling is not thread-safe and can corrupt or lose staged offsets. Offsets should be collected by the worker threads and flushed from `poll()` on the main thread instead.

close() does not flush remaining committable offsets or drain queues

`close()` sets `shutdown_event`, joins the commit thread and shuts the pool down. The commit loop exits as soon as the event is set, so any work completed in the last interval (and any work the workers finish during their 5s join) is never committed. Queued-but-unprocessed items are also dropped by `queue.shutdown(immediate=False)`? they are drained only if workers keep up within the join timeout. On every consumer shutdown/rebalance this causes re-delivery (duplicate processing) of up to a second's worth of already-processed results, and silently dropped work if workers don't finish. A final `get_committable_offsets()`/commit after draining is needed.

queue.ShutDown / Queue.shutdown require Python 3.13+

`queue.ShutDown` and `queue.Queue.shutdown(immediate=...)` were only added in Python 3.13. On any older interpreter this module raises `AttributeError` at worker-exception handling time and `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` logs "Error shutting down queue" for every queue while workers stay blocked in `get()` forever, so the consumer can never shut down. If the runtime is not guaranteed to be 3.13+, this needs a compatibility path (e.g. sentinel items).

Decode/grouping failures mark the offset complete and are silently dropped

In `submit()`, any exception from the decoder or `grouping_fn` is caught, logged, and the offset is immediately added+completed, i.e. the message is committed as if processed. There is no DLQ handling and no metric, so malformed or unexpected payloads are permanently lost with only a log line. Consider routing these to the DLQ (raise `InvalidMessage`) or at least emitting a counter.

Per-partition lock map and defaultdicts mutated without a global lock

`_get_partition_lock` and the `defaultdict` accesses in `add_offset`/`get_committable_offsets` mutate `self.partition_locks`, `self.all_offsets` and `self.outstanding` from multiple worker threads plus the commit thread with no guarding lock (the per-partition lock is acquired only after the dict lookup/creation). This relies entirely on CPython dict/`setdefault` atomicity and will break under free-threaded builds or if the implementation changes. A single mutex guarding the maps (or a lock around lock-creation) would make the invariants explicit.

hash() of group key is not stable across processes

`get_queue_for_group` uses builtin `hash(group_key)`, which for `str` is salted per process (PYTHONHASHSEED). The docstring claims "consistent hashing", but assignment differs between consumer processes and across restarts. This is tolerable since each process owns distinct partitions, but if ordering guarantees are ever expected to hold across processes/restarts this is wrong; use a stable hash (e.g. md5/crc32) instead.

WorkItem retains full Kafka message for no reason

`WorkItem.message` stores the entire arroyo `Message` (including the raw payload bytes) but is never read anywhere; partition/offset are tracked separately. With unbounded queues this doubles the memory held per queued item. Drop the field.

Flaky assertion that 20 groups hit all 3 queues

`test_different_groups_distributed` asserts `len(queue_indices) == 3` based on `hash()` of 20 group keys, which is randomized per process. It is likely but not guaranteed that all three queues are hit, so this test can fail intermittently. Assert `>= 2` or seed a deterministic hash.

join() ignores its timeout argument

`join(timeout)` discards `timeout` and calls `close()`, which uses hard-coded 5s joins for the commit thread and each worker. With N queues this can block for N*5s during shutdown, exceeding arroyo's join timeout and triggering a forced kill mid-processing. The timeout should be honoured/budgeted across the threads.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. Concurrent cold-start requests will each serialize on the mutex and redundantly parse/fetch the manifest (including an HTTP request in the CDN case) even though an earlier goroutine already populated the cache.

Also, the limit is applied only for SQLite; other drivers have their own limits (e.g. Postgres allows at most 65535 bind parameters), so a batch size above that would fail at runtime on Postgres. false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit request context and get cancelled

All four goroutines (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163) build their timeout context from the incoming request ctx (`context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`). The apiserver cancels the request context as soon as the HTTP handler returns, which typically happens before the goroutine completes. The legacy write will then fail with context canceled, silently dropping the legacy copy that mode 3 exists to maintain. Use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (preserving auth/user values) as the parent before applying the timeout.

Storage error path records legacy duration metric

In Create, when `d.Storage.Create` fails the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` even though the failing call was to unified storage. Same in Update (line 129). This mislabels failures: storage error rates/latencies will be missing and legacy metrics will be polluted with storage failures. Should be `recordStorageDuration`.

DeleteCollection legacy goroutine records storage duration

The goroutine measuring the legacy DeleteCollection calls `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` instead of `recordLegacyDuration`, so legacy delete-collection latency/errors are never recorded and storage metrics are double-counted with legacy timings.

Legacy Update receives the raw objInfo, re-applying the patch against the legacy object

The previous implementation wrapped objInfo with the already-updated object (`updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}`) before calling legacy. Now the raw `objInfo` is passed, so legacy will call `UpdatedObject` against its own stored object. For patch/apply requests this can produce a different result than what was written to unified storage (and resourceVersion precondition checks are evaluated against legacy's RV), causing the two stores to diverge or the legacy update to fail with a conflict.

Tests never synchronize with the async legacy write

Mode 3 now performs the legacy write in a goroutine, but the tests return immediately after the storage call. Nothing asserts that Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection is invoked, so the core behaviour of this PR is untested. Worse, the shared `mock.Mock` is read/written by the goroutine after the test function finishes, which is a data race (will fail under -race) and can cause 'mock called after test completion' panics. Add a synchronization hook (e.g. a channel/WaitGroup signalled from the mock's Run function) and assert the legacy calls.

Local registry shadows package-level one inconsistently

`p := prometheus.NewRegistry()` inside TestMode3_Get shadows the package-level `p` used by every other test here, while the mode1 test removed exactly this pattern. All other subtests reuse one global registry across many NewDualWriter calls; if the metrics registration uses MustRegister this repeated registration of the same collectors will panic. Pick one approach (fresh registry per test is safest) and apply it consistently.

These look like accidental local-tooling churn and should be dropped from the PR.

Callers that already interpolate before calling runSplitQuery (shard splitting, and any datasource.query path that pre-processes targets) will now have variables/ad-hoc filters applied a second time. There is no guard or flag to opt out, so the function's contract silently changed: passing pre-interpolated targets is no longer safe. Consider adding an option (e.g. `skipInterpolation`) or documenting/enforcing that callers must pass raw targets.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.

Count-then-insert is not atomic, limit can be exceeded

CreateOrUpdateDevice reads the device count and then inserts in a separate statement/session. Concurrent anonymous requests (or multiple Grafana instances sharing the DB) can all observe count < deviceLimit and each insert, so the stored device count can exceed the configured device_limit. A transaction with appropriate locking, or an atomic INSERT ... SELECT guarded by the count, is needed if the limit is meant to be enforced.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race condition: concurrent requests can pass a non-atomic device count check and insert devices beyond the limit. Both suggest transactional locking or atomic enforcement.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

rowsAffected==0 wrongly treated as device limit reached on MySQL / unchanged rows

updateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached whenever the UPDATE affects 0 rows. With MySQL (default CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS off) an UPDATE that matches an existing row but sets identical values reports 0 affected rows, so an already-registered anonymous device whose client_ip/user_agent/updated_at are unchanged would be denied authentication even though it is within the limit. The error is also semantically wrong for the 'device not found' case; a known device should succeed. Consider checking existence explicitly (SELECT) instead of relying on rows affected.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same incorrect mapping of zero affected rows to ErrDeviceLimitReached and explicitly notes that a missing device does not indicate a reached limit. Its additional MySQL unchanged-row scenario does not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
localCache is populated before the store write, letting over-limit devices bypass the limit

tagDeviceUI calls a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{}) before CreateOrUpdateDevice. If the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached (and the request is therefore rejected in Anonymous.Authenticate), the device id is nevertheless cached, so for the next ~29 minutes tagDeviceUI returns nil early and the same unknown device is granted anonymous access without ever being recorded. The limit is effectively bypassed by retrying. The cache should only be set after a successful write.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: tagDeviceUI caches the device ID before CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds, leaving the cache entry intact after ErrDeviceLimitReached and allowing retries to bypass the device limit for approximately 29 minutes.

false_positives.candidate:
Device tagging moved onto the request path adds a DB count+write per anonymous request

TagDevice was previously executed in a background goroutine with its own timeout; it is now called synchronously inside Authenticate. For every anonymous request that misses the local cache this now performs a SELECT COUNT(*) on anon_device plus an upsert before the request can proceed, and any DB latency/failure directly affects anonymous page loads. Under high anonymous traffic with a configured limit this COUNT query over a large table is a notable added cost.

Raw ErrDeviceLimitReached returned from Authenticate yields an unhelpful 500/opaque error

ErrDeviceLimitReached is created with fmt.Errorf and returned directly from Authenticate. The authn layer expects typed errutil errors to produce a correct HTTP status and user-facing message; a plain error will surface as a generic internal error rather than a clear 'anonymous device limit reached' response, and gives no way for the frontend to show the limit message implied by the new anonymousDeviceLimit frontend setting.

New auth.anonymous device_limit option not documented in defaults.ini/sample.ini or docs

cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit is read from [auth.anonymous] device_limit, but no entry was added to conf/defaults.ini, conf/sample.ini, or the configuration docs. Users have no discoverable way to learn about the setting or its default (0 = unlimited), and Grafana convention is that every ini option is listed in defaults.ini.

ProvideAnonDBStore signature change may break wire DI registration

ProvideAnonDBStore now takes an extra int64 argument and AnonDeviceService constructs the store itself instead of receiving anonstore.AnonStore. If ProvideAnonDBStore is still registered as a provider in pkg/server/wire.go (not included in this PR), wire will fail to build because there is no provider for int64, and any other consumer of the injected AnonStore loses it. Verify the DI graph was updated.

Device limit tests do not cover the update path for an existing device at the limit

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only asserts that a *new* device id is rejected once the limit is hit. There is no test that an already-registered device still succeeds (updates its updated_at/client_ip) when the limit is reached — exactly the path that is broken by the rowsAffected==0 logic on MySQL/unchanged rows. Add a case re-tagging the existing device id after the limit is reached.

true_positives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
ensure_loaded!/@loaded_locales initialization is not thread-safe

`I18n.ensure_loaded!` reads and lazily initializes `@loaded_locales` outside `LOAD_MUTEX` (only `load_locale` takes the lock). Under concurrent requests on a threaded server, two threads can simultaneously see nil/stale arrays and `@loaded_locales << locale` from different threads can lose entries, causing redundant loads or a locale being considered loaded while its translations are only partially installed. Perform the check and initialization under the same mutex.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify unsynchronized lazy initialization and concurrent access to @loaded_locales as the thread-safety issue. The candidate explicitly notes that initialization occurs outside LOAD_MUTEX and recommends synchronization.

false_positives.candidate:
SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym can raise NoMethodError

`[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en]` calls `to_sym` on the setting value before any nil check. If `SiteSetting.default_locale` is nil or blank (e.g. during early boot, before site settings are provisioned, or in a DB-less/migration context), this raises `NoMethodError: undefined method 'to_sym' for nil`. Since this method is invoked on every I18n fallback lookup and from `ensure_loaded!` in a before_filter, a single nil setting breaks all translation. The trailing `.compact` cannot help because the exception happens while building the array; guard with `SiteSetting.default_locale.presence&.to_sym` instead.

Translation LRU cache key ignores fallback locales

The cache key is `"#{key}#{config.locale}#{config.backend.object_id}"`. With the new Fallbacks backend, the resolved value for a given key/locale also depends on `SiteSetting.default_locale` (the second entry of FallbackLocaleList). After an admin changes the site default locale, previously cached entries resolved through the old fallback remain in the LRU cache and are served, producing stale/incorrect translations until a process restart or `I18n.reload!`. The fallback chain (or default_locale) should be part of the cache key, or the cache must be invalidated when default_locale changes.

Fallback locales only loaded in web requests; jobs/mailers get missing translations

`I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` is only called from `ApplicationController#set_locale`. Because `translate` lazily loads only `config.locale`, any code path outside a controller request (Sidekiq jobs, mailers, rake tasks, console, console-driven digests) performing a lookup in a locale with a missing key will have the fallback locale's YAML not loaded, so the Fallbacks backend finds nothing and raises/returns a missing-translation instead of the fallback string. The loading should be hooked into the lookup path (e.g. inside `translate`/`load_locale`) or into the job/mailer locale setup as well.

translate can NoMethodError on nil @loaded_locales

`translate` does `@loaded_locales.include?(config.locale)` without initializing `@loaded_locales`, while the newly added `ensure_loaded!` defensively does `@loaded_locales ||= []`. If any translation happens before `reload!` has run (the only place that initializes the ivar), `translate` raises `NoMethodError` on nil. Initialize the ivar consistently (e.g. `@loaded_locales ||= []` in `translate` too) rather than relying on call ordering.

No tests for fallback behaviour

This PR introduces a new fallback chain (user locale -> site default locale -> :en) plus lazy loading of fallback locale files, but adds no specs. There is no coverage asserting that a key missing in the user locale resolves from the site default locale and then from English, nor that fallback locale YAML is actually loaded before lookup. Given the silent-failure mode (missing translation strings shown to users), a spec for FallbackLocaleList#[] and an end-to-end translation fallback spec should be added.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

The HTML should be sanitized/whitelisted before being stored as cooked.

import mutates the caller's contents string

`contents << "\n<hr>..."` appends in place to the string passed in by the caller. Callers that reuse or cache the string (e.g. retrying the import, or passing a frozen/literal string) will see the footer appended repeatedly, or get a RuntimeError on a frozen string. Build a new string instead (`contents = contents + ...`).

create_table with force: true in migrations can drop existing tables

`create_table :topic_embeds, force: true` (and the same change made to 20131223171005_create_top_topics.rb) issues a DROP TABLE IF EXISTS before creating. If the table already exists on an installation, running the migration silently destroys its data. Migrations should not use `force: true`.

content_sha1 updated even when revise! fails

`revisor.revise!` can return false (e.g. `should_revise?` false) or `@post.save` can fail validation silently, yet `embed.update_column(:content_sha1, content_sha1)` runs unconditionally. The embed then records the new checksum while the post still holds the old content, so the update will never be retried on subsequent imports. Only update the sha when the revision actually succeeded.

false_positives.candidate:
Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure despite the docstring

`FixedQueuePool.__init__` creates `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, and `submit()` never raises `MessageRejected`. The class docstring for `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but nothing ever blocks or rejects: if a worker is slow, the consumer keeps reading from Kafka and buffering decoded results in memory without bound, which can OOM the consumer and also inflates offset-tracking state. A bounded queue plus raising `MessageRejected` (or blocking put) is needed to get the advertised backpressure.

queue_pool is created once per factory and destroyed by strategy close(), breaking rebalances

The `FixedQueuePool` (and its worker threads and `OffsetTracker`) is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__`, but `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`terminate()` call `queue_pool.shutdown()`, which stops all worker threads and shuts down the queues. Arroyo calls `create_with_partitions` again after every rebalance/partition revocation. On the second call, `assert self.queue_pool is not None` still passes (the attribute isn't cleared by the strategy), so a new strategy is built on top of dead workers and already-shutdown queues: submitted work is never processed and offsets are never committed, stalling the consumer silently. Additionally the `OffsetTracker`'s `last_committed`/`all_offsets` are carried across assignments, so stale per-partition state can suppress commits (or commit offsets for partitions no longer owned) after a rebalance. The pool should be created per `create_with_partitions` call (or reset on revocation).

Arroyo commit callback invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs in its own thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which is arroyo's `commit` callback passed to `create_with_partitions`. That callback (and the underlying consumer offset staging) is expected to be invoked from the main processing thread; calling it concurrently with the StreamProcessor's `poll`/`submit`/commit handling is not thread-safe and can corrupt or lose staged offsets. Offsets should be collected by the worker threads and flushed from `poll()` on the main thread instead.

close() does not flush remaining committable offsets or drain queues

`close()` sets `shutdown_event`, joins the commit thread and shuts the pool down. The commit loop exits as soon as the event is set, so any work completed in the last interval (and any work the workers finish during their 5s join) is never committed. Queued-but-unprocessed items are also dropped by `queue.shutdown(immediate=False)`? they are drained only if workers keep up within the join timeout. On every consumer shutdown/rebalance this causes re-delivery (duplicate processing) of up to a second's worth of already-processed results, and silently dropped work if workers don't finish. A final `get_committable_offsets()`/commit after draining is needed.

queue.ShutDown / Queue.shutdown require Python 3.13+

`queue.ShutDown` and `queue.Queue.shutdown(immediate=...)` were only added in Python 3.13. On any older interpreter this module raises `AttributeError` at worker-exception handling time and `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` logs "Error shutting down queue" for every queue while workers stay blocked in `get()` forever, so the consumer can never shut down. If the runtime is not guaranteed to be 3.13+, this needs a compatibility path (e.g. sentinel items).

Decode/grouping failures mark the offset complete and are silently dropped

In `submit()`, any exception from the decoder or `grouping_fn` is caught, logged, and the offset is immediately added+completed, i.e. the message is committed as if processed. There is no DLQ handling and no metric, so malformed or unexpected payloads are permanently lost with only a log line. Consider routing these to the DLQ (raise `InvalidMessage`) or at least emitting a counter.

Per-partition lock map and defaultdicts mutated without a global lock

`_get_partition_lock` and the `defaultdict` accesses in `add_offset`/`get_committable_offsets` mutate `self.partition_locks`, `self.all_offsets` and `self.outstanding` from multiple worker threads plus the commit thread with no guarding lock (the per-partition lock is acquired only after the dict lookup/creation). This relies entirely on CPython dict/`setdefault` atomicity and will break under free-threaded builds or if the implementation changes. A single mutex guarding the maps (or a lock around lock-creation) would make the invariants explicit.

hash() of group key is not stable across processes

`get_queue_for_group` uses builtin `hash(group_key)`, which for `str` is salted per process (PYTHONHASHSEED). The docstring claims "consistent hashing", but assignment differs between consumer processes and across restarts. This is tolerable since each process owns distinct partitions, but if ordering guarantees are ever expected to hold across processes/restarts this is wrong; use a stable hash (e.g. md5/crc32) instead.

WorkItem retains full Kafka message for no reason

`WorkItem.message` stores the entire arroyo `Message` (including the raw payload bytes) but is never read anywhere; partition/offset are tracked separately. With unbounded queues this doubles the memory held per queued item. Drop the field.

Flaky assertion that 20 groups hit all 3 queues

`test_different_groups_distributed` asserts `len(queue_indices) == 3` based on `hash()` of 20 group keys, which is randomized per process. It is likely but not guaranteed that all three queues are hit, so this test can fail intermittently. Assert `>= 2` or seed a deterministic hash.

join() ignores its timeout argument

`join(timeout)` discards `timeout` and calls `close()`, which uses hard-coded 5s joins for the commit thread and each worker. With N queues this can block for N*5s during shutdown, exceeding arroyo's join timeout and triggering a forced kill mid-processing. The timeout should be honoured/budgeted across the threads.

If any translation happens before `reload!` has run (the only place that initializes the ivar), `translate` raises `NoMethodError` on nil. Initialize the ivar consistently (e.g. `@loaded_locales ||= []` in `translate` too) rather than relying on call ordering.

This PR introduces a new fallback chain (user locale -> site default locale -> :en) plus lazy loading of fallback locale files, but adds no specs. There is no coverage asserting that a key missing in the user locale resolves from the site default locale and then from English, nor that fallback locale YAML is actually loaded before lookup. Given the silent-failure mode (missing translation strings shown to users), a spec for FallbackLocaleList#[] and an end-to-end translation fallback spec should be added.
